title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM-Generated Network Configuration Changes
abstract: We report a preregistered, paired experimental study that measured whether deterministic tool-augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → optional repair) reduces unsafe network-change proposals produced by a hosted LLM in intent-to-configuration NetOps tasks. We ran N=200 preregistered synthetic intent-to-configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM-only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Primary confirmatory outcome: paired difference in unsafe-proposal rate (guarded minus baseline). Observed result: baseline unsafe rate = 0/200, guarded unsafe rate = 0/200 (paired risk difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% CI on difference 0.0–0.0). Interpretation: in this controlled synthetic benchmark both pipelines produced no verifier-detected unsafe proposals; therefore the guarded pipeline did not reduce unsafe proposals here. We discuss causes (preregistered shared-generation semantics, synthetic tasks, ceiling effect), operational implications, and concrete design changes for future NetOps-specific adversarial and production-scale evaluations. All experiment artifacts, preregistration, verifier, and analysis code are archived per the execution manifest; limitations and scope are stated explicitly.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operator efficiency but raises operational-safety concerns: an erroneous configuration can violate reachability, break services, or cause outage. Prior work proposes tooling around LLMs—retrieval, deterministic validators, sandbox simulators, and guarded execution gates—to raise operational trust (surveys and prototypes: e.g., Bilal et al. (arXiv:2605.12729), Okula (TechRxiv), and broader tool-augmented studies). However, reproducible, preregistered NetOps-focused experiments that quantify the effect of deterministic verifier pipelines under benign and adversarial prompts are scarce. Our research question: does deterministic tool-augmentation reduce the rate of unsafe configuration proposals from an LLM in a controlled, preregistered paired experiment? Contributions: (1) a machine-readable preregistration and deterministic synthetic NetOps task generator; (2) a paired confirmatory execution (N=200) comparing baseline LLM-only and a guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5) under preregistered benign and adversarial prompt clusters; (3) analysis and diagnostics showing a null paired difference in this setting, and an evidence-grounded discussion of causes and next steps.
sections.related_work: LLM use in NetOps/AIOps has rapidly expanded from feasibility prototypes to architectural treatments arguing for tool grounding, verification-in-the-loop, and governance (surveys and position work; e.g., Bilal et al., arXiv:2605.12729; Ferrag et al., 6G-Bench DOI:10.1109/ojcoms.2026.3680457). Empirical studies in adjacent high-stakes domains show that tool-augmentation and verifier-assisted pipelines can increase measured correctness and evidence support (e.g., domain-aggregated tool-augmented evaluations, SSRN:10.2139/ssrn.7132138). Method proposals such as generate–verify–refine / divide–verify–refine aim to reduce constraint violations (recent experimental work and method papers). Architectural proposals emphasise governance layers (MCP/schemas, execution gates, audit trails) as necessary for operational reliability (several 2025–2026 prototypes and position papers). Yet prior literature also highlights that measured benefits are task- and verifier-dependent and that static QA benchmarks are insufficient—motivating our preregistered, workflow-centred paired experiment (see references in cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (study_id cand-2026-01-prereg-v1; preregistration hash archived) before execution. Confirmatory hypothesis H1: tool-augmentation reduces unsafe-proposal rate in the adversarial prompt cluster (paired binary estimand: guarded minus baseline). Sampling and tasks: deterministic synthetic topology/task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 distinct tasks (seeded generator); tasks targeted IPv4 reachability, route-filtering/ACL predicates, and ordered workflow constraints (shutdown→change→restore patterns). Execution contract: paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics (generation_semantics: shared_initial_candidate; independent_condition_generation=false) so a single initial LLM candidate was shared across both arms per task, then passed to the guarded verifier when applicable. Model and orchestration: model declared as gpt-5-mini via the openai_responses adapter; orchestration and execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Guarded pipeline: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executed full intent-constraint validation in a sandboxed deterministic validator/simulator (validator traces archived). Analysis plan: primary test = McNemar-style paired exact test on paired binary outcomes (unsafe proposal present =1, absent=0); primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; alpha=0.05 (Bonferroni when reporting both clusters). Pre-specified exclusions, retries, stopping rules, and sensitivity analyses are documented in the preregistration and execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution summary: planned paired episodes = 400 (200 tasks × 2 conditions). Completed episodes = 400; model calls used = 200 (shared-generation design). Primary confirmatory results (adversarial prompt cluster): baseline unsafe proposals = 0/200; guarded unsafe proposals = 0/200. Paired contingency (n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Paired risk difference (guarded minus baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. 95% CI on the paired difference (paired bootstrap percentile, resamples=10000, seed=1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Secondary/diagnostic outputs: refusal rate and verifier ROC diagnostics were preregistered as exploratory; in this run no verifier refusals or discordant cases occurred so no empirical ROC curve is produced. All raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived (see execution_manifest and analysis_artifacts). Representative example episodes and validator traces are available in the archived bundle (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json).
sections.discussion: The observed null paired difference reflects that, for the sampled synthetic tasks and the shared-generation semantics used here, both pipelines produced zero verifier-detected unsafe proposals. This outcome can arise for multiple, evidence-grounded reasons: (1) ceiling effect in the synthetic task bank: task constructions and reference intents may have favored correct candidate generation; (2) experimental-generation semantics: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate design intentionally fixed the LLM candidate across conditions (to control generation noise and model-call budget), which produced identical initial outputs for baseline and guarded arms and therefore prevented observing verifier-mediated differences when the initial candidate was already valid; (3) adversarial prompt strength and coverage: although an adversarial cluster was preregistered, the specific adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from the chosen model on the synthetic tasks; (4) single-model scope: results apply only to the declared model (gpt-5-mini) and the validator implementation used. Comparison to prior literature: while tool-augmentation has been reported to improve correctness in other domains and datasets (see SSRN:10.2139/ssrn.7132138 and related studies), our controlled null result shows that (a) a guarded pipeline cannot improve correctness if candidates are already valid, and (b) experimental design choices (shared-generation vs independent generation) materially affect the ability of confirmatory tests to detect pipeline differences. Operational implication: evaluators must avoid ceilinged task banks and must choose generation semantics aligned to the hypothesis (e.g., independent per-condition generation to permit guardrails to alter outcomes). Suggested next steps: repeat with independent generation per arm, stronger and systematically varied adversarial prompts, multiple LLMs, and a broader set of topology/intent patterns; stress-test the verifier with intentionally camouflaged obfuscation patterns and record verifier false-negative cases for targeted improvements.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM-only baseline to a deterministic verifier-augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Both arms produced zero verifier-detected unsafe proposals in this run (paired risk difference 0.0; p=1.0). This null result does not contradict prior evidence that tool-augmentation can help; rather it highlights how task design and generation semantics determine whether a verifier can demonstrably reduce unsafe outputs. Future NetOps evaluations should (a) avoid ceiling effects, (b) use independent-condition generation when testing verifier impact, (c) include stronger adversarial cases and multiple models, and (d) report verifier operating characteristics and human-operator cost trade-offs. Our archived artifacts, preregistration, and code are intended to support these next steps and reproducible follow-up studies.

limitations: Synthetic-task domain and coverage: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single-AS multi-device setups (generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5); results may not generalize to production, multi-AS, or vendor-specific features.

Shared-generation semantics: the preregistered design used shared_initial_candidate per paired task (independent_condition_generation=false). This produced identical initial candidates for baseline and guarded arms, producing a ceiling effect when those candidates were valid and preventing observation of verifier-driven differences in those cases.

Adversarial prompt strength: although an adversarial cluster was preregistered, the adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt-5-mini on the sampled tasks; more diverse and stronger adversarial cases are needed.
Single-model scope: only gpt-5-mini (declared) was evaluated; no claims of multi-model generality are supported.

Verifier validation scope: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 operated deterministically on the synthetic sandboxed states archived; external independent validation of validator completeness against all real-world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator-in-the-loop workload measurement, nor multi-vendor interoperability field trials were performed; operator-cost trade-offs (false refusals, extra verification workload) remain unquantified at scale.
